# Roadmap

What the template is for: a new BFO/CCO ontology repository with the method and checks of
the Business Capability Ontology (BCO) on its first commit, without copying the last
project's tools by hand. Each phase ends at a gate the architect holds; its conditions are
written below before the phase starts.

Sources weighed in planning it, 2026-10-23: the BCO repository (the tooling carried here),
the ODK project-setup tutorial (for capabilities ODK projects get that the BCO did not
have), [IRI_Linter](https://github.com/Skreen5hot/IRI_Linter) (for inclusion), and the
layered ontology pipeline associated with Jessica Talisman (controlled vocabulary, metadata
schemas, taxonomy, thesaurus, ontology, knowledge graph), as a layout a colleague brought --
weighed for what each layer adds, not adopted as a directory structure (see "Layers
compared with the ontology pipeline", below).
Decisions: [`DECISIONS.md`](DECISIONS.md).

## 1. Extract and generalize the core

Carry the BCO's generic tooling, take every project-specific value out of it, and make
starting a project one command.

- `config/project.yaml` holds the id, code, title, namespace, prefix, IRI base and repository;
  every tool reads it through `tools/project.py`.
- `tools/init_project.py` turns a copy into a project; `tools/project.py --check` (first in
  CI) fails a copy that was never initialized.
- `tools/template_status.py` and `config/template-manifest.json`: digests of every
  template-owned file, so a project can see where it diverged and what a newer template
  changed.
- BFO is vendored whole (`select: all`), so its hierarchy is available before any term
  names it; CCO is vendored by reference, as in the BCO.
- Not carried: the BCO's specification, review, v0.1 draft, BPO pin, import inventory,
  communications record, and public site (phase 7).

**Gate:** the suite and every CI step pass in the template; a test runs init in a copy and
checks the result describes itself (layout, namespace, project file); a test fails if a
template-owned file names BCO, BPO or APQC; a full init with regeneration has been run once
and its suite passed.

## 2. Upstreams

- More than one file per source (the BCO's HANDOFF §5.2 gap).
- Sister ontologies (BPO, BCO, ARO) as optional pins, documented with a worked entry.
- `config/upstream-register.json`, generated by vendoring: every IRI and label in the full
  pinned BFO and CCO, so phase 3 can suggest the opaque IRI for a readable-label mistake
  offline.

**Gate:** the weekly `--confirm` job passes; a test adds a second file to a constructed
source and sees it vendored and attributed.

Built 2026-10-23: `files:` per source, `vendor/<id>/<id>-register.json` (role
`vendored-register`; BFO 76 terms, CCO 1,995 -- all of CCO, so "Organization" resolves to
`cco:ont00001180` offline), digest-checked offline and byte-checked by `--confirm`, and a worked
BPO entry, commented out, at the end of `config/upstream-sources.yaml`. Neither pinned
upstream marks any term `owl:deprecated`, so the register's deprecation flag is exercised on
a constructed source only.

## 3. IRI lint

Port IRI_Linter's rules to Python rather than vendor it: it needs Node and a vendored N3.js,
its register is hand-kept, it skips unparseable files silently, it covers CCO only, and its
scheme rule is APQC-specific. Keep its JSON output and its exit codes (0/1/2), with a parse
failure as exit 2. Rules: `unverified`, `readable_label` (with the opaque IRI suggested),
`case_mismatch`, `dangling_ref`, `redeclared_upstream`, `deprecated_upstream`. Run it in CI,
as a pre-commit hook, and as a Claude Code hook on `.ttl` edits. Credit IRI_Linter in the
notice.

**Gate:** a fixture breaks each rule and a positive control passes it; a parse failure exits 2.

Assessed before porting, 2026-10-23 (cloned, its 128 assertions run, probed with
constructed files): the rules were right, and four defects made the code unusable for a
BFO/CCO project -- `obo:` treated as project-minted, so every BFO parent was a dangling
reference; an unparseable file reported clean, exit 0; a register from a 2026-04-04 CCO, so
114 CCO v2.0 terms were "unverified" and 34 it accepted are not in v2.0; and the first line
of an IRI reported for every occurrence. Each is a test case in
`tests/fixtures/iri_lint/`. Built as `tools/ontology/iri_lint.py`, reading the phase-2
registers; wired into CI, a git pre-commit hook (`.githooks/`), and a Claude Code
PostToolUse hook (`.claude/settings.json`). One addition the plan did not name: a readable
name is matched against the other upstream too (`cco:Process` -> `obo:BFO_0000015`).
After the gate, the three things the suite cannot show were run for real (recorded in
`docs/HANDOFF.md` §4): `deprecated_upstream` against IAO, which deprecates 24 terms (no
pinned upstream deprecates any); the git hook refusing and accepting real commits; and the
Claude Code hook handing a finding back to an agent in a live session.
IRI_Linter is credited in the tool's docstring and DEVELOPMENT.md rather than in
`vendor/NOTICE.md`: no code or data of it is redistributed, only its rules and test ideas,
rewritten.

## 4. Realist shape library and competency questions

One shape set, with its fixture, per rule:

- every authored class reaches a BFO root through `rdfs:subClassOf`;
- exactly one asserted named parent;
- no class under two disjoint BFO categories (continuant and occurrent; independent and
  dependent);
- upstream terms are neither redeclared nor annotated in authored modules;
- genus-differentia definitions ("An X is a G that…"), as a warning;
- domain and range respected for BFO/CCO relations used in restrictions;
- the ontology header: title, licence, version IRI, creator;
- deprecated terms carry a replacement or a reason;
- the annotation profile (CCO's `skos:definition` and the rest) set in `config/project.yaml`.

Competency questions, beside the shapes because they are the other half of "is this
ontology right": a shape says what must never be true, a competency question says what the
ontology must be able to answer.

- `competency-questions/`, one file per question: id, the question in words, status
  (`draft` | `answerable` | `deferred`), the terms it depends on, a SPARQL query, and the
  expected answer;
- a check that runs every `answerable` question's query against the authored ontology plus
  the vendored extracts and fails on a wrong answer, gated against a baseline like the
  shapes;
- a fixture of questions built to fail (a wrong expected answer; a query that selects
  nothing) so a question that passes because it asks nothing is caught;
- the terms the questions name are vendoring seeds, as the shapes' are;
- `examples/`: small instance graphs (ABox) the questions are answered against, one per
  scenario, each saying which questions it serves. A question can only be answered over
  individuals, and an ontology with no instances answers every "which X ..." with nothing.
  Example individuals are held to the same rules as the modules: the IRI linter runs over
  them, every type they assert is an authored or a pinned class, and they are in a namespace
  of their own under the project (`<iri_base>/examples/`), so they are never counted as terms
  of the ontology or published in its base release.

**Gate:** each constraint is listed by message in a test and fires on its fixture; positive
controls conform. Fixtures that need BFO in scope load the BFO extract. A competency
question with a wrong expected answer fails the check, and one whose query matches nothing
is refused rather than passed. An example individual typed with a class nothing declares is
refused.

Built 2026-10-23. What changed from the plan, and why:

- **Derived disjointness.** BFO states the disjointness a realist check leans on hardest --
  independent, specifically dependent and generically dependent continuant; process and
  the regions -- only as five `owl:AllDisjointClasses` axioms, blank-node lists the extract
  drops. Without more, "no class under two disjoint categories" could never catch its own
  headline case. The vendoring tool now writes `vendor/bfo/bfo-disjointness.ttl`: those
  axioms as the 21 pairwise `owl:disjointWith` triples they are equivalent to, labelled as
  derived. A test shows the independent/dependent case passes without that file and fails
  with it.
- **"Upstream terms not annotated" is a linter rule, not a shape** (`annotated_upstream`):
  a shape sees the merged graph and cannot tell an authored triple from a vendored one.
- **Severity belongs to a shape.** pyshacl ignores `sh:severity` on a SPARQL constraint
  node; the first draft's four warnings all came out as violations, and the fixture run
  showed it. Warnings now live in a node shape of their own, and the ladder reports them
  without gating them.
- **No competency-question baseline.** `status` already says which questions are expected
  to pass; an answerable question that fails is a failure, and a known gap is a `draft`.
- **The annotation profile is its own file** (`config/annotation-profile.yaml`), generating
  `shapes/annotation_profile_shapes.ttl`; default, CCO's *definition source*, as a warning.
- **Fixtures run with the extracts in scope**, so a fixture class can sit under a real BFO
  category.
- **Query shape.** The first range check did not finish in 60 seconds: a property path
  separated from its binding pattern by a FILTER ran over every node. Rewritten; the ladder
  takes about 17 seconds. And a WHERE made only of filters, with `$this` pre-bound, is
  evaluated oddly by rdflib (`{ FILTER(false) }` returned every focus node), so every
  constraint binds `$this` in a triple pattern first.

## 5. Reasoning and release

In a CI job of its own (decision 2):

- a pinned ROBOT jar with its digest checked;
- ELK over the authored modules plus the full pinned upstreams (cached, not committed):
  consistency and unsatisfiable classes;
- deterministic release artefacts — base (authored only) and full (merged), a version IRI
  stamped from the tag, TTL, OWL and JSON-LD — and a GitHub release with checksums.

**Gate:** a fixture with an unsatisfiable class fails the job; two builds of one tag are
byte-identical.

Built 2026-10-23. ROBOT v1.9.10 (sha256 `16a73c07...`, tag commit `c7c03529`), chosen over
the three-week-old v1.9.11; actions pinned by SHA from the GitHub API (setup-java v6.0.1,
cache v6.1.0). Measured first: BFO + CCO v2.0 + the module reason clean with ELK in about
11 seconds, and ELK over the full upstream catches the independent/dependent case the
shapes need the derived disjointness for. Two things the plan did not foresee:

- **rdflib's RDF/XML and JSON-LD writers are not deterministic** across processes, even for
  a canonicalised graph inserted in sorted order (measured across three hash seeds). The
  release tool writes both itself, flat and sorted; Turtle stays rdflib's, which measured
  stable. Every file is parsed back and required to be its source graph, and ROBOT (the OWL
  API) loads the hand-written `.owl` and `.jsonld`.
- **ROBOT's unsatisfiable dump is a module, not a list** -- it carries the BFO context
  classes too -- so the unsatisfiable classes are read from ROBOT's log, and a run whose
  count line and named classes disagree is refused rather than read as "none".
- The **full** release is asserted axioms only (authored plus the vendored extracts it was
  checked against), not reasoned, so it stays deterministic and Python-built; the reasoner
  gates the release instead.

Not exercised end to end: the Release workflow publishing to GitHub. It refuses to run in
the template (whose ontology is a placeholder), so its first real run is a project's first
tag -- phase 8.

## 6. Authoring ergonomics, vocabulary and governance, crosswalks

- a Protégé `catalog-v001.xml`, so imports resolve to the vendored extracts offline;
- a canonical-form check for authored modules, because Protégé reserializes files on save;
- pre-commit, Dependabot for the SHA-pinned actions, issue and PR templates, CITATION.cff;
- TSV-to-Turtle term generation (ROBOT-template style), its output declared generated;
- semantic diff of authored terms as a PR comment;
- **the vocabulary layer**: `vocabulary/terms.tsv`, the intake for domain experts who do not
  write Turtle -- term, preferred label, definition, synonyms, proposed parent, source,
  requester -- turned into Turtle by the TSV-to-Turtle step above, its output declared
  generated. A row is a proposal until a reviewer sets its status; only accepted rows are
  generated;
- **a SKOS concept-scheme module type**, for vocabularies that are about terms rather than
  types -- catalogs, code lists, taxonomies of business usage -- with shapes for the scheme's
  structure: every concept `skos:inScheme` a declared scheme, top concepts declared,
  `skos:broader` acyclic and within one scheme, an `altLabel` or `hiddenLabel` never
  duplicating a `prefLabel`. Kept apart from the OWL hierarchy on purpose: a concept is not a
  universal, and no OWL class is generated from one;
- **governance**: `docs/governance/` with the naming convention (label casing, local-name
  form), the deprecation policy (`owl:deprecated` plus a replacement or a reason, enforced by
  the phase-4 shape), a term-request issue template, and a change log generated from the
  corpus between releases rather than kept by hand;
- **crosswalks**: `mappings/*.sssom.tsv`, mappings to external standards in SSSOM, the OBO
  community's mapping format, with its metadata block (mapping set id, licence, creator). A
  check requires every subject to be a declared authored term, every object to fall in a
  namespace the mapping set declares, every predicate to be a SKOS mapping property or
  `owl:equivalentClass`, and `skos:exactMatch` only between things of one kind (class to
  class, concept to concept). Mappings are not loaded into the ontology graph: an
  `exactMatch` to a vocabulary that is not BFO-aligned would otherwise become a claim about
  the ontology's types;
- `research/`: the project's own notes and summaries of sources, with a README saying what
  goes there and what does not. Project content under the project licence. The sources
  themselves, when licensed, stay in `docs/Reference/`, which is never tracked; a test
  refuses a research note that embeds a file from there.

Built 2026-10-24, in three commits (6a authoring aids, 6b vocabulary and governance, 6c
crosswalks), each through CI on a scratch branch first. What changed from the plan:

- **Pre-commit** was already done in phase 3 (`.githooks/`); not repeated.
- **The Protégé entry point** is a generated `protege/edit.ttl` importing every module and
  vendored file, with the catalog beside it -- the modules themselves import nothing,
  because vendoring replaces imports. ROBOT (the OWL API) loads it through the catalog
  offline; its first catalog did not load, for a `--` inside an XML comment.
- **The canonical-form check is opt-in** (`format: canonical` on a module): canonical form
  keeps no comments, and a hand-written module's reasoning lives in them.
- **The semantic diff and the change log are one tool** (`term_diff.py`): a PR comment from
  the Term diff workflow, and `CHANGES.md` in every release, inside the checksums.
- **Naming is a linter rule** (`naming_convention`, patterns in `config/naming.yaml`); label
  casing is left to each project's `docs/governance/naming.md`, because BFO and CCO differ.
- **A concept-scheme module is an ordinary module**: the SKOS shapes apply to every authored
  concept and scheme wherever written, so no new module type was needed.
- **Crosswalks to BFO or CCO are refused**: relating a term to the foundation is an axiom.
- **init `--offline`**: every generator but the vendoring rebuild.

## 7. Public site

Carry the BCO's site whole -- the documentation an ontology pipeline would generate with
PyLODE or Widoco, here a checked and reproducible build: `tools/site/build_site.py` and
`check_site.py`, the page
fragments, copy and assets (stylesheet, explorer and ranking scripts), and
`.github/workflows/pages.yml` -- build, check, prove the build reproducible, deploy from the
artifact the checks ran against, preview artifacts on pull requests. Generalized: every
project value from `config/project.yaml`, the spec and review pages optional (rendered when
a `specification` component exists), a competency-question page (each question and whether
it is answered), a crosswalk page (the SSSOM mappings, by target), a vocabulary page (concept
schemes, browsable as trees), and a release page. Documented in DEVELOPMENT.md: enabling Pages, the
local preview, what the build refuses. `Markdown` is pinned again in the commit that adds
it.

**Gate:** the BCO's site tests, generalized, pass in the template and in an initialized
copy; two builds are byte-identical; the workflow deploys the template's own site once.

Built 2026-10-24. What changed from the plan:

- **Publishing is the default, and a private repository is never linked** (decision 10):
  `"publish": true` in `site/content/site.json` from the first commit; every run builds,
  checks and proves the build reproducible whatever it says. Built for a private
  repository, the site writes no link into it, and the checker refuses one.
- **The spec and review pages** are built from any component with role `specification` or
  `review`; the suite builds them from stand-in components so a project without either still
  has them tested.
- **The explorer's ranking is run under Node** on the shipped file, where the BCO's suite
  did not run it at all.
- **The footer composes its notices** from the project file, the pins and `LICENSE`; the
  curated file says only whether the site is a draft, whether IRIs resolve, and whom else to
  credit.

## 8. Prove it

A CI job in the template initializes a copy with sample values, adds one term under a CCO
class, rebuilds the extracts, and runs the whole gate — showing the suite is not vacuous.
Then a real "Use this template" run, to green CI, in one sitting.

## Capabilities compared with ODK

| ODK | Here |
|---|---|
| one project config (`odk.yaml`) | `config/project.yaml` (phase 1) |
| seeding (`odkrun seed`) | `tools/init_project.py` (phase 1) |
| import management | seeds derived from the corpus, extracts pinned and digest-checked; BFO whole |
| full-fidelity imports (SLME) | phase 5's reasoning job, over the full pinned upstreams |
| reasoning | phase 5 |
| ROBOT report (QC) | wellformedness shapes now; the realist library in phase 4 |
| release artefacts | phase 5 |
| Protégé catalog, normalization | phase 6 |
| ROBOT templates, DOSDP | phase 6 (TSV to Turtle) |
| ID ranges | not needed: readable local IRIs (decision 4) |
| mkdocs | phase 7, a checked and reproducible site, with its Pages workflow |
| (no ODK counterpart) | competency questions as checked queries over example instances (phase 4); a research record (phase 6) |
| mappings (SSSOM) | crosswalks in `mappings/`, checked, kept out of the ontology graph (phase 6) |
| Docker | not used: a pinned Python environment, plus a pinned ROBOT jar in phase 5 |

## Layers compared with the ontology pipeline

The pipeline a colleague brought, attributed to Jessica Talisman: six layers from controlled
vocabulary to knowledge graph, as numbered directories. Weighed here for what each layer
contributes; its layout is not adopted, for the reasons in the last column. DEVELOPMENT.md
will carry this table, so someone who knows the pipeline can find each layer.

| Pipeline layer | Here | Not adopted, and why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 controlled vocabulary (`terms.csv`, expert intake) | `vocabulary/terms.tsv`, a review status, generated Turtle (phase 6) | -- |
| 2 metadata schemas (LinkML, SHACL) | SHACL shapes now; the realist library (phase 4) | LinkML as the source of truth: it generates schema-shaped, closed-world OWL rather than BFO-anchored types, and would bypass the checks on authored Turtle. Fine for a data-exchange schema built on the ontology, in another repository |
| 3 taxonomy (SKOS schemes) | concept-scheme modules with structural shapes (phase 6) | Deriving the OWL hierarchy from it. In a realist ontology the `rdfs:subClassOf` tree under BFO is the classification of types; a SKOS scheme is a vocabulary about terms, kept beside it, never upstream of it |
| 4 thesaurus (altLabel, related, crosswalks) | SKOS labels in concept schemes; SSSOM crosswalks (phase 6) | -- |
| 5 ontology (OWL, imports, axioms) | `ontology/`, the pinned vendored extracts, reasoning (phase 5) | Imports by git submodule or download script: the pinned, digest-checked extracts are stronger |
| 6 knowledge graph (RML mappings, instances, competency queries) | `examples/` instances and competency questions (phase 4) | RML/R2RML lifting pipelines: they belong to an application repository built on the ontology, not to the ontology's template |
| numbered stage directories | roles in the layout contract | A numbered order says the ontology is built from the taxonomy. The layers coexist; the contract's roles say what each file is and what is checked |
| CI with `robot.jar` from "latest" and tag-pinned actions | a pinned ROBOT jar with its digest (phase 5); actions pinned to commit SHAs | Unpinned tools make a check's result depend on the day it ran |
| PyLODE / Widoco documentation | the phase-7 site | -- |
